_README: Cuisine regions, eating customs, dish glossary (names and one-line meaning only, no recipes or menu text), street-food safety, from DK 2015 pp242–245 and p266. Paraphrase only.

regions.claim: Three culinary regions: NORTH simpler and less sweet, cooler-climate, home of pho and bun cha, exotic meats and snake wine; CENTRE spicier, with Hue's imperial multi-course tradition and the country's strongest vegetarian (Buddhist) cooking; SOUTH sweeter and more tropical, coconut, curries, Khmer/Thai/Indian touches.
Chinese legacy: chopsticks, soy sauce, tofu, stir-frying; French: baguette, coffee, dairy, pâté; Cham/Indian rhythms in the south.
Rice is the centre of the language and the plate: everyday non-sticky rice vs glutinous rice for festivals; rice flour becomes noodles, rice paper, cakes; distilled rice becomes rice wine.
Frog, snake, snails, turtle, sparrows and — in the north — dog appear on menus; some places serve banned wild species. An American reader needs the vocabulary to avoid them, not a lecture.
regions.verify_against: Hanoi's 2018 campaign to curb dog meat; current prevalence in tourist districts

regions.claim: LP's thesis: travelling north to south is a journey that 'begins in China and ends in Southeast Asia'. North: Chinese imprint, mild, soy as often as fish sauce, vinegar for sourness instead of lime or tamarind, black pepper instead of chilli, long cooking. Centre: balance and moderation except for chilli; everything smaller (mini baguettes and herbs); Hue's imperial dishes dainty; shrimp sauce (mam tom) and lemongrass. South: abundance and sweetness, coconut milk, big-leaf herbs, tamarind, goi salads of papaya, pomelo and lotus stem.

Every cook balances hot, sour, salty and sweet. Salt comes from nuoc mam: anchovies layered with salt and fermented up to a year; the first extraction is table-grade, the second (salt water added) is for cooking; Phu Quoc is the famous origin, Phan Thiet milder. Sugar via caramel in clay-pot kho braises; sourness from lime, kalamansi, tamarind (south) or vinegar (north).

Vietnam uses less chilli than Thailand except in the centre, where Hue's small pale-green chilli 'really packs a punch'; Vietnam is a huge pepper exporter and its black peppercorns outclass supermarket pepper — half a kilo makes an edible souvenir.

venues.claim: The venue ladder: white-tablecloth restaurants (big cities, hotels) → specialist sit-downs built around one dish (bun thit nuong, banh xeo, lau hotpot) → quan com point-at-the-glass-case rice shops, often six seats → pho shops → pushcarts and yoke vendors with a charcoal stove.
Choose the street stall packed with locals on plastic stools; 'com bui' (dusty food) is the affectionate name for street eating.

Bia hoi is Hanoi's preservative-free draught beer, brewed daily and drunk the same day in hole-in-the-wall bars on tiny stools; southern beer gardens rotate promoted brands weekly and serve DIY spring rolls.
DK says pho connoisseurs come LATE to a stall for a stronger, more reduced broth.
venues.verify_against: Most Hanoi guidance says the opposite (go early before the broth and the best cuts run out). Treat as a book claim, not a fact.

venues.claim: Hotel-run half-day classes with a market visit (Metropole, Hanoi) and Hoi An's long-running Miss Vy class were the 2015 benchmarks; culinary tours (HCMC→Hoi An→Hue→Hanoi) cover the three regional styles in about a week.
venues.verify_against: Whether both classes still run and at what price

venues.claim: A Hanoian's eating day: bun rieu cua (paddy-crab noodle soup) for breakfast, strong coffee or iced lemon tea mid-morning, bun cha at lunch (the classic Hanoi midday meal), banh goi fried pastries in the afternoon, bia hoi with roast duck or dried squid at dusk.

Three meals: breakfast is noodles or chao; lunch is social with workmates at a stall or local restaurant; dinner leisurely with family; constant snacking in cities. No courses — dishes land in the middle as they are ready and a host may drop morsels into your bowl on a special occasion. The kitchen has its own deity, Ong Tao, whose altar is the room's most important object.

By 2016 street-food tours ran in HCMC (Vespa/XO by night), Hoi An, Danang, Hue, Hanoi and Dalat; LP's advice for a first night is a Vietnamese 'showcase' restaurant (Quan An Ngon-style) to learn the dishes before the stools.

Cooking courses have 'really taken off', most with a market visit; Hoi An hosts the most (Morning Glory, Red Bridge, Green Bamboo); Hanoi Cooking Centre runs children's classes; HCMC has a chef-led school; Sapa's Hill Station teaches Hmong-influenced dishes.

Coffee is a phin-drip ritual over condensed milk on a tiny stool that 'can't be rushed'; the menu: ca phe sua da (iced with condensed milk), ca phe da (iced black), ca phe den (black), ca phe sua chua (yoghurt coffee), ca phe trung (egg coffee); heritage cafés in Hanoi (Duy Tri, Pho Co) and K'Ho's minority-grown coffee near Dalat.

Bia hoi for 'a pittance'; Saigon, Huda and central-coast La Rue decent bottled beers; craft beer since 2016; Hanoi vodka 'dirt-cheap'; ruou rice liquor flavoured with herbs, fruit or animals; ruou can communal straw wine in the highlands; snake wine uses officially endangered snakes. Tea is a ritual of hospitality (hot green in the north, iced in the south; lotus, jasmine, chrysanthemum); sugar-cane juice with kalamansi; sinh to smoothies; che sweet soups.

Com chay restaurants sit near Buddhist temples with mock-meat tofu and gluten; on the 1st and 15th of each lunar month many vendors go vegetarian — the easy days; otherwise assume fish sauce or shrimp paste in any vegetable dish. The Vietnamese are 'voracious omnivores'.

Goat hotpot, frogs, paddy crabs (bun rieu), golf-ball snails (bun oc, lemongrass-stuffed), snakehead, catfish, central-coast clams; seafood restaurants keep the catch live in tanks as the freshness guarantee; 15 grades of dried shrimp at market; dried squid barbecued from roving carts.

LP's honest line: pho gets the press, but truly fine versions with a carefully made broth are hard to come by; northern purists frown on adding lime, basil or sprouts; the broth is beef bones boiled for hours with shallot, ginger, fish sauce, black cardamom, star anise and cassia.

Restaurants are the biggest diarrhoea risk; eat freshly cooked food, avoid shellfish and buffets, peel fruit, prefer cooked vegetables and busy high-turnover places; tap water no, city ice generally yes.

customs.claim: No courses: dishes arrive as cooked; order one dish per head plus one for the table; everyone shares; slurping and bone-dropping are normal in local places; loud is friendly.

Dedicated vegetarian restaurants were few in 2015 but avoiding meat is easy; the trap is nuoc mam (fish sauce) in almost everything — vegans must say so explicitly. Hue is the vegetarian capital; the Buddhist tradition produces meat-free versions of classic dishes with tofu and mushrooms.
customs.note: 'Toi an chay' = I eat vegetarian; 'an chay' restaurants have multiplied since.

customs.claim: The book warns bland-diet travellers that Vietnamese food can be spicy enough to upset the stomach; carry antacids.
Bottled or boiled water; tea is safe because it is boiled; peel fruit yourself; watch buffets and room service even in top hotels.
